Only future credits after the order
The clear balance available with the garnishee at the time of receipt of the order
The average balance of the last 6 months

The individual account of the partner/director

questions.q: If a Garnishee Order and an Attachment Order are received simultaneously or are pending for payment, which gets preference?
questions.explain: The table states 'Attachment order will have the preference over Garnishee Order.'

To make sure financial institutions hold enough capital to meet obligations and absorb unexpected losses
To fix interest rates for member countries

questions.q: What does NRE stand for?
questions.explain: The material defines the 'Non-Resident External (NRE) account'.

questions.q: Which account lets an NRI deposit foreign currency earnings and freely repatriate the money to their country of residence?
questions.explain: An NRE account is 'a savings account in which you can deposit foreign currency earnings and freely repatriate monies held in the account back to your country of residence'.

questions.q: In which currency are the funds in an NRE account maintained?
options: The currency of the country of residence
questions.explain: 'NRE accounts are INR denominated accounts which means all the funds you deposit are maintained in Indian rupee.'

questions.q: When foreign currency is deposited into an NRE account:
options: It is converted to rupees at the current exchange rate applied by the receiving bank
It is converted at a fixed RBI rate set once a year
It is kept in the foreign currency
questions.explain: 'When you deposit foreign currency into this account, the current exchange rate is applied by the receiving bank and Indian rupees matching the exchange rate are deposited.'

questions.q: Which statement about the money in an NRE account is correct?
options: It is repatriable only up to USD 1 million a year
It is completely repatriable and tax-free
questions.explain: Key feature: 'The money you deposit in this account is completely repatriable and tax-free'.

questions.q: According to the material, up to what interest rate can be earned on an NRE savings account?
questions.explain: 'You can earn up to 3.5% p.a. interest rate on your savings account and up to 5.75% p.a. interest rate on your NRE deposits.'

questions.q: According to the material, up to what interest rate can be earned on NRE deposits?
questions.explain: The material gives 'up to 5.75% p.a. interest rate on your NRE deposits'.

questions.q: What does NRO stand for?
questions.explain: The material defines the 'Non-Resident Ordinary (NRO) account'.

questions.q: Which account is meant for an NRI's earnings in India, such as dividends, pension and rent?
questions.explain: The NRO account 'is useful if you have earnings in India ... dividends, equity returns, pension, rentals, or any other income'.

questions.q: In which currency can withdrawals be made from an NRO account?
options: In INR or USD, at the customer's choice
questions.explain: Key feature of the NRO account: 'Withdrawals can only be made in INR'.

questions.q: How much can be repatriated from an NRO account each financial year?
questions.explain: 'You can repatriate up to USD 1 million every financial year from this account.'

questions.q: In which currency is an NRO account maintained?
questions.explain: 'Similar to an NRE account, NRO Account is maintained in INR too.'

questions.q: What does FCNR (B) stand for?

questions.q: An FCNR (B) account lets an NRI save money earned overseas:
options: In INR, as a current account
In a foreign currency, as a term deposit
In INR, as a savings account
questions.explain: FCNR(B) 'allows you to save money earned overseas in a foreign currency in a term deposit'.

questions.q: Which of the following currencies is listed for FCNR deposits?
questions.explain: The listed currencies are USD, GBP, AUD, CAD, SGD and HKD.

questions.q: What is the tenure range of FCNR deposits?
questions.explain: 'The tenure of these deposits can range between 1 year and 5 years.'

questions.q: In an FCNR account, which of the following is fully repatriable?
options: Both the deposit amount and the interest earned
questions.explain: 'The amount you deposit and the interest earned are fully repatriable.'

questions.q: What happens to an FCNR deposit on maturity, per the material?
options: It is moved to an NRO account
It must be closed and paid in INR
questions.explain: 'FCNR account allows automatic renewal of deposit on maturity.'

questions.q: How are FCNR deposits taxed in India?
options: They are not taxable in India
They are taxed like NRO deposits
questions.explain: The material states 'FCNR deposits are not taxable in India'.

questions.q: Which account is described as 'Our Account with You'?
questions.explain: An account kept by an Indian Authorised Dealer with a foreign bank is called a 'NOSTRO' account, 'meaning Our Account with You'.

questions.q: Which is the example given of a Nostro account?
options: Bank of India's USD account with Citibank
Canara Bank's account referred to by SBI at BNP New York
Citibank's rupee account with Bank of India
An NRI's savings account in India
questions.explain: The material gives the example 'BOI's USD ACCOUNT WITH CITI BANK'.

questions.q: Which account is described as 'Your Account with us'?
questions.explain: Foreign correspondent banks' rupee accounts with Indian banks are called 'VOSTRO' accounts, 'meaning Your Account with us'.

questions.q: Which is the example given of a Vostro account?
options: Citibank's rupee account with Bank of India
Bank of India's USD account with Citibank
SBI's account with BNP New York
questions.explain: The material gives the example 'CITI BANK RUPEE ACCOUNT WITH BANK OF INDIA'.

questions.q: Why do foreign correspondent banks keep Vostro accounts with Indian banks in rupees?
questions.explain: Foreign banks keep rupee accounts with Indian banks 'for the purpose of settling their rupee transactions'.

questions.q: How is the Loro account described?
options: An NRI's foreign currency term deposit
Their money: an account held by a second bank on behalf of a third party
questions.explain: The slide shows 'Loro Account (Their money)', described as 'a record of an account held by a second bank on behalf of a third party'.

questions.q: In practice, when is a Loro account mainly used?
questions.explain: 'In practice this is rarely used, the main exception being complex syndicated financing.'

questions.q: How many types of international current account are shown in the material?
options: Four: Nostro, Vostro, Loro and NRE
questions.explain: The slide 'Three types of International Current account' lists Nostro (our money with you), Vostro (your money with us) and Loro (their money).

questions.q: What does SWIFT stand for?
options: Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication
Society for World Investment and Financial Trade
System for Worldwide International Fund Transfer
questions.explain: The material expands SWIFT as 'Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication'.

questions.q: When was SWIFT founded, and where is its headquarters?
questions.explain: SWIFT was 'Founded in 1973, headquartered in Brussels, Belgium'.

questions.q: What is SWIFT?
options: A worldwide financial messaging network for banks and financial institutions
A foreign currency deposit scheme for NRIs
A central bank for international settlements
questions.explain: SWIFT 'is a worldwide financial messaging network where messages are securely and reliably exchanged between banks and other financial institutions'.

questions.q: Which rules allow banks to pay dues to nominees after a depositor's death, without asking for a succession certificate?
questions.explain: The introduction states 'Banking Companies (Nomination) Rules 1985 permits banks to pay dues to nominees in the event of death of depositor(s) without asking for succession certificate'.

questions.q: On what date was the nomination facility introduced in the Banking Regulation Act, 1949?
questions.explain: 'Nomination facility was introduced on 29th March 1985 in the Banking Regulations Act, 1949'.

questions.q: Which sections of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 deal with nomination?
questions.explain: Nomination is covered by 'Sec 45-ZA to 45-ZF' of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949.

questions.q: For which of these is the nomination facility available?
options: Deposit accounts, safe custody accounts and safe deposit lockers
questions.explain: 'Nomination are available for: 1) Deposit Accounts 2) Safe Custody Accounts and 3) Safe Deposit vault accounts'.

questions.q: Which section of the BR Act covers acceptance of nomination for deposits?
questions.explain: The table lists Section 45-ZA for acceptance of nomination for deposits, and Section 45-ZB for paying only to nominees.

questions.q: Which section of the BR Act covers acceptance of nomination for safe custody articles?
questions.explain: The table lists Section 45-ZC for acceptance of nomination for safe custody, and Section 45-ZD for delivery only to nominees.

questions.q: Which section of the BR Act covers delivery to nominees of the contents of safe deposit lockers?
questions.explain: The table lists Section 45-ZE for acceptance of nomination for safe deposit lockers, and Section 45-ZF for delivery only to nominees.

questions.q: What is the maximum number of nominees allowed for a deposit account?
questions.explain: Nomination can be made in favour of 'One or more individual but not exceeding Four, either successively or Simultaneously'.

questions.q: In whose favour can a nomination NOT be made?
questions.explain: The nomination must be 'in favour of one or more individual ... not in favour of Trust, Society etc.'

questions.q: How many nominees can be registered for a gold collateral loan (single account)?
questions.explain: The 'Number of Nominees in Bank' table lists 'One Person Only' for a single Gold Collateral Loan.

questions.q: How can nominees be registered for safe custody articles?
options: Up to four individuals, successively only
Up to four individuals, simultaneously only
questions.explain: 'The facility of nomination is available in case of deposit of safe custody articles by One or more individual but not exceeding Four by successively.'

questions.q: Which of these government deposit schemes allows more than one nominee?
questions.explain: The material lists Government Deposit Schemes that allow more than one nominee: PPF, Sukanya Samriddhi Scheme, Senior Citizen Saving Scheme, PF, Gratuity etc.

questions.q: Which nomination form is used to register a nomination for a deposit account?
questions.explain: For deposits, the forms are DA 1 (registration), DA 2 (cancellation) and DA 3 (variation).

questions.q: Which nomination form is used to cancel a nomination for a deposit account?
questions.explain: For deposits, DA 2 is the form for cancellation of nomination.

questions.q: Which nomination form is used to vary (change) a nomination for a deposit account?
questions.explain: For deposits, DA 3 is the form for variation of nomination.

questions.q: Which form is used to register a nomination for a joint safe deposit locker account?
questions.explain: For safe deposit lockers, registration is SL 1, or 'SL 1A (JOINT A/C)'.

questions.q: What is the main benefit of nomination?
options: Funds/articles are released faster, without insisting on a succession certificate or probate
The account can never be closed
The nominee becomes the owner of the deposit
questions.explain: 'Nomination facilitates faster and easier release of funds/articles without insistence on Succession Certificate / Probate of Will.'

questions.q: For whom is the nomination facility intended?
questions.explain: 'Nomination facility is intended for individuals and sole proprietary concerns.'

questions.q: In which of these accounts can a nomination NOT be made?
questions.explain: Nomination cannot be made where deposits are held in a representative capacity, e.g. Trust accounts, Partnership Firms, HUF, Companies, Associations, Clubs etc.

questions.q: In a joint account of individuals, who must make the nomination?
questions.explain: 'In case of a joint account of individuals, nomination should be made by all depositors jointly.'

questions.q: Can a non-resident be nominated in a resident account? If so, where is the amount credited?
options: Yes; the amount is paid only in cash
Yes; the amount is credited to the nominee's NRO account
Yes; the amount is credited to the nominee's NRE account
questions.explain: 'A non-resident can be nominated as a nominee in a resident account ... will be credited to his NRO account.'

questions.q: Can a minor make a nomination in a self-operated minor account?
options: Yes, but only for term deposits
No; a minor cannot make a nomination
Yes, a minor can make any nomination
Yes, but only with RBI approval
questions.explain: 'Minor can not make a nomination in self operated minor accounts.' In a guardian-operated minor account, the guardian can make the nomination.

questions.q: When a minor is made the nominee, what condition applies?
options: The deposit must be frozen until the minor turns 18
The account holder must appoint another adult to receive the amount on the minor's behalf if the depositor dies during the nominee's minority
A minor can never be a nominee
questions.explain: Nominating a minor is allowed 'on the condition that the account holder ... appoints another individual, not being a minor, to receive the amount ... during the minority of the nominee'.

questions.q: Does a nomination made under the Arrears of Pension (Nomination) Rules, 1983 also cover the pensioner's bank deposit accounts?
options: Yes, but only for the pension account
Yes, it covers all bank accounts automatically
No; a separate nomination is needed under the Banking Companies (Nomination) Rules, 1985
questions.explain: The two sets of rules are distinct. A pension-arrears nomination 'will not be valid for the purpose of deposit accounts ... a separate nomination is necessary'.

questions.q: What happens to a nomination when a term deposit is renewed?
options: It continues in force unless specifically cancelled or changed
It moves to the bank's discretion
questions.explain: 'A nomination will continue to be in force even on renewal of term deposit, unless specifically cancelled or changed.'

questions.q: What is noted on the FDR/passbook after a nomination is registered?
options: 'Nomination registered', without the nominee's name unless the customer asks for it
The nominee's full name and address
questions.explain: A notation 'Nomination registered' is made, and the 'Name of nominee will not be mentioned except when it is specifically requested by customer'.

questions.q: What must happen if the holder of a single-name account does not want to nominate?
options: The bank nominates a legal heir
The refusal must be given in writing
questions.explain: 'Nomination is compulsory in all single named accounts. Where the account holder is not willing to nominate, he/she is to give his/her refusal in writing.'

questions.q: How is the account holder's execution of the nomination form attested?
options: A signature needs two witnesses; a thumb impression needs none
A thumb impression needs two witnesses; a signature needs no attestation
questions.explain: The forms require 'thumb impression of the account holder ... to be attested by two witnesses. RBI has clarified that signature need not be attested.'

questions.q: After a nomination, cancellation or variation form is filed, what must the bank do?
options: Publish the nominee's name in a newspaper
Acknowledge the filing in writing to the depositor(s)
questions.explain: 'The banking company shall acknowledge in writing, to the concerned depositor or depositors, the filing of the relevant duly completed Form of nomination or cancellation of nomination or variation of nomination.'

questions.q: What is the legal status of a nominee after the depositor's death?
options: A trustee for the legal heirs, who is not the owner and cannot operate the account
The absolute owner of the deposit
A joint account holder with full operating rights
questions.explain: 'The nominee is treated as a Trustee for Legal Heirs ... He is not owner. He does not acquire right of a depositor. He can't operate the account.' On payment to the nominee, the bank is discharged from liability.

questions.q: On what date was the Reserve Bank of India established?
questions.explain: The introduction states the RBI was 'established on 1 April 1934'.

questions.q: From what date was the RBI nationalised?
questions.explain: The RBI was 'nationalized with effect from 1st January, 1949' under the Reserve Bank of India (Transfer to Public Ownership) Act, 1948.

questions.q: Which section of the RBI Act, 1934 makes the Reserve Bank the nation's sole note-issuing authority?
questions.explain: 'Sec. 22 of RBI Act, 1934, The Reserve Bank is the nation's sole note issuing authority.'

questions.q: Who is the issuing authority for coins in India?
options: The Security Printing and Minting Corporation
questions.explain: 'The Government of India is the issuing authority of coins and supplies coins to the Reserve Bank on demand.'

questions.q: Under which section of the RBI Act has the RBI set up an agency system of currency chests and small coin depots with banks?
questions.explain: The material refers to 'Section 45 of the RBI Act, 1934' for the agency system of currency chests and small coin depots.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT listed among the banks appointed as RBI agents for currency chests?
questions.explain: The agents listed are SBI and Associates, Public Sector Banks, Private Sector Banks, Co-operative banks, Foreign Banks and RRBs.

questions.q: Who approves the design and pattern of bank notes?
options: The Government of India, on the RBI's recommendation
questions.explain: 'Design and pattern of notes recommended by RBI & approved by Government of India.'

questions.q: Which note is issued by the Government of India rather than the RBI?
questions.explain: Notes of Rs. 2 to Rs. 500 are issued by the Reserve Bank of India, and the Re 1 note by the Government of India.

questions.q: Under which law are Re 1 notes issued?
questions.explain: 'Re. 1/- notes issued in terms of Currency Ordinance 1940.'

questions.q: Under which Act are coins issued?
questions.explain: The material states 'Coins are issued in terms of Indian Coinage Act 1906' and can be issued up to Rs. 1000.

questions.q: What is the highest denomination in which notes can be issued, per the material?
questions.explain: Notes may be issued in denominations 'not exceeding ten thousand rupees'.

questions.q: Under which section of the RBI Act must coins be circulated only through the RBI?
questions.explain: 'Coins to be invariably circulated through RBI only in terms of Sec 38 of RBI Act.'

questions.q: Which of these is a currency note press?
questions.explain: The presses are at Nasik, Dewas, Mysore and Salboni; the mints are at Mumbai, Hyderabad, Kolkata and Noida.

questions.q: How many presses and mints are shown in the note and coin distribution chain?
questions.explain: The distribution chart shows '4 Presses', '4 Mints', '20 RBI Offices' and the currency chests.

questions.q: Who destroys withdrawn coins?
questions.explain: The disposal chart states 'Withdrawn coins are destroyed by Mints', while soiled notes are sent to the RBI for processing and destruction.

questions.q: How many branches of 'our bank' are linked with currency chests of IB, SBI, IOB, KVB and CBI?
questions.explain: '35 branches of our bank linked with IB, SBI, IOB, KVB & CBI currency chests.'

questions.q: How many notes make a packet, and how many packets make a bundle?
options: 100 notes make a packet; 10 packets make a bundle
50 notes make a packet; 20 packets make a bundle
1,000 notes make a packet; 10 packets make a bundle
100 notes make a packet; 5 packets make a bundle
questions.explain: '100 Notes of same denomination forms a Packet; 10 Packets forms one bundle.'

questions.q: What service charge per packet applies at currency chests, per the material?
questions.explain: 'Service Charge is Rs. 5/- per packet (98306 – Agency Commission).'

questions.q: How should soiled notes be packed?
options: Mixed with good notes in the same bundle
Separately, marked 'Soiled – Not for Reissue', using banding and no stapling
In loose bags with no marking
questions.explain: The material says 'Use Banding; No stapling' and 'Soiled notes should be packed separately and marked Soiled – Not for Reissue'.

questions.q: Up to what limit must banks exchange soiled notes free of charge, per customer per day?
questions.explain: 'Soiled notes should be accepted and exchanged up to 20 Pieces or Rs. 5000/- per day per customer at free of charge.'

questions.q: Under the Note Refund Rules, 2009, what is a 'soiled note'?
options: A note that has become dirty from normal wear and tear, including a two-piece note pasted together from the same note
A note formed from halves of two different notes
A note made of more than two pieces
A note with a portion missing
questions.explain: A soiled note 'has become dirty due to normal wear and tear and also includes a two piece note pasted together wherein both the pieces ... belong to the same note'.

questions.q: A note with a portion missing, or made of more than two pieces, is called:
questions.explain: 'Mutilated banknote is a banknote, of which a portion is missing, or which is composed of more than two pieces.'

questions.q: A note formed by joining half of one note to half of another note is called:
questions.explain: 'Mismatched Note – a note which has been formed by joining a half note of any one note to a half note of another note.'

questions.q: For mutilated notes up to Rs. 20, what value is paid when the single largest undivided piece is more than 50% of the note?
questions.explain: For notes up to Rs. 20: area > 50% gives full value; area equal to or below 50% is rejected.

questions.q: For mutilated notes of Rs. 50 and above, what value is paid if the largest undivided piece is between 40% and 80% of the area?
questions.explain: For Rs. 50 and above: below 40% is rejected; 40% to 80% gets half value; above 80% gets full value.

questions.q: Under ultraviolet light, what colour does the security thread fluoresce on Rs. 10, Rs. 20 and Rs. 50 notes?
questions.explain: The thread in Rs. 10, 20 and 50 notes 'fluoresces in yellow'. Rs. 100 and above have a thread that shifts from green to blue.

questions.q: How many angular bleed lines are on the Rs. 500 note?
options: 4 lines with two circles in between
questions.explain: 'Angular Bleed Lines ... 4 lines in 2 blocks in Rs. 100, 4 angular bleed lines with two circles in between in Rs. 200, 5 lines in 3 blocks in Rs. 500.'

questions.q: On which notes is the numeral printed in colour-shifting ink (green to blue)?
questions.explain: 'The numeral 200 & 500 on the Rs. 200 & Rs. 500 banknotes are printed in a colour-shifting ink.'

questions.q: Which identification mark for the visually impaired is on the Rs. 100 note?
questions.explain: The marks are: Rectangle – Rs. 20, Square – Rs. 50, Triangle – Rs. 100, Circle – Rs. 500, Symbol H – Rs. 200.

questions.q: What escort is required for a cash transit above Rs. 50 lakhs and up to Rs. 5 crores?
options: One officer and one armed guard
Two staff and one armed guard
A bank cash van with at least two staff (one an Office Assistant (MP) or Officer) and two armed guards
questions.explain: Above Rs. 50 lakhs up to Rs. 5 crores: 'Cash Van of the bank should be accompanied by at least two staff ... and two armed guards.' Above Rs. 40 lakhs up to Rs. 50 lakhs needs two staff and one armed guard.

questions.q: Which trust administers the CGFMU scheme?
options: Credit Guarantee Fund Trust for Micro and Small Enterprises
questions.explain: The comparison lists the trust for CGFMU as the 'National Credit Guarantee Trustee Company (NCGTC)'.

questions.q: What does CGTMSE stand for?
options: Credit Guarantee Fund for Micro Units
Credit Guarantee Trust for Medium and Small Enterprises
Credit Guarantee Fund Trust for Micro and Small Enterprises
questions.explain: The comparison names the trust 'Credit Guarantee Fund Trust for Micro and Small Enterprises (CGTMSE)'.

questions.q: When was CGTMSE introduced?
questions.explain: The 'Introduced on' row gives 01.08.2000 for CGTMSE and 18.04.2016 for CGFMU.

questions.q: When was CGFMU introduced?
questions.explain: The 'Introduced on' row gives 18.04.2016 for CGFMU.

questions.q: What is the purpose of CGFMU?
options: Insuring deposits up to Rs. 5 lakh
Guaranteeing housing loans to salaried borrowers
Guaranteeing payment against default in micro loans given by banks, NBFCs, MFIs and other intermediaries
questions.explain: CGFMU is for 'Guaranteeing payment against default in Micro Loans extended to eligible borrowers by Banks/NBFCs/MFIs/Other Financial Intermediaries'.

questions.q: Up to what loan amount are micro loans in manufacturing/services (including retail trade) eligible under CGFMU?
questions.explain: Eligible CGFMU activities include 'Micro loans up to Rs. 20.00 lakh under Manufacturing/Services sector including retail trade'.

questions.q: Which activities are eligible under CGTMSE?
options: All MSE activities under the new MSME definition, including trading and educational/training institutions
questions.explain: CGTMSE covers 'All MSE activities as per new definition of MSME (It includes Trading activity) and Educational/Training Institution'.

questions.q: Which of the following is eligible under CGFMU but not mentioned under CGTMSE?
questions.explain: CGFMU's eligible activities include 'OD facility under PMJDY', along with agri-allied loans and SHG/JLG loans.

questions.q: Can collateral security be obtained for loans covered under CGTMSE and CGFMU?
options: No; it must not be obtained under either scheme
questions.explain: The 'Collateral security' row says 'Not to be obtained' for both schemes.

questions.q: Under which scheme is the hybrid/partial collateral option available?
questions.explain: The hybrid/partial collateral option (part covered by collateral, the rest collateral-free) is 'Available' under CGTMSE and 'Not Available' under CGFMU.

questions.q: What is the maximum guarantee cover under CGTMSE?
questions.explain: Maximum guarantee cover: 'Up to Rs. 200.00 Lakhs' for CGTMSE and 'Up to Rs. 20 Lakhs' for CGFMU.

questions.q: In which situation is the credit guarantee NOT applicable under either scheme?
options: If the borrower is a woman entrepreneur
If a third-party guarantee is available
If the borrower is a new enterprise
If the unit is in the North East Region
questions.explain: Credit guarantee does not apply where guarantee cover is already available, if collateral is obtained, or if a third-party guarantee is available.

questions.q: Under CGTMSE, what fee concession applies to each category (Women/SC/ST/PWD, NER up to Rs. 50 lakh, ZED certified)?
options: 10% each, up to a maximum discount of 30%
5% each, up to a maximum of 15%
15% each, up to a maximum of 45%
25% for all, as a flat discount
questions.explain: Each category gets a 10% concession, and an MSE in all three categories gets the maximum discount of 30%.

questions.q: What does ZED stand for in the CGTMSE fee concession?
questions.explain: The annexure notes '# ZED – Zero Effect Zero Defect'.

questions.q: Under CGTMSE, what is the standard Annual Guarantee Fee rate for credit facilities up to Rs. 10 lakhs?
questions.explain: The AGF slabs give a standard rate of 0.37% (0.33% after discount) for up to Rs. 10 lakhs.

questions.q: Under CGTMSE, what is the standard AGF rate for credit facilities above Rs. 100 lakhs and up to Rs. 200 lakhs?
questions.explain: The slab above Rs. 100 lakhs up to Rs. 200 lakhs has a standard rate of 1.20% (1.08% after discount).

questions.q: Under CGFMU, what is the annual guarantee fee for SHG loans in the first year?
questions.explain: CGFMU AGF: 'All categories except SHG – 1.00% pa; SHG – 0.25% 1st year, 0.50% 2nd year'.

questions.q: Under CGFMU, what risk premium applies when the NPA percentage in the guaranteed portfolio is 0–2%?
questions.explain: The CGFMU risk premium table lists 0–2% NPA as 'NIL', >2–3% as 10% of SR, and so on up to 50% of SR for >12–15%.

questions.q: When can CGTMSE guarantee cover be taken?
options: Only after the account becomes NPA
Only at the time of sanction
Any time during the loan tenure, if the facility was not restructured or in SMA-2 in the last 1 year
questions.explain: CGTMSE cover can be initiated 'Anytime during the tenure of loan provided the credit facility was not restructured/remained in SMA 2 status in the last 1 year'.

questions.q: Under CGFMU, within how many days of receiving the Demand Advice must the AGF be paid?
questions.explain: For CGFMU, 'AGF is to be paid within 3 days from the date of receiving Demand Advise.' For CGTMSE it is paid immediately.

questions.q: By what date must the CGTMSE Annual Service Fee (ASF) be paid each year?
options: On or before 15th April (or another date CGTMSE specifies)
questions.explain: The ASF demand advice is generated by the 2nd week of February and must be paid 'on or before 15th April every year'.

questions.q: On what basis is the CGTMSE Annual Service Fee calculated?
options: Outstanding balance for term loans, sanctioned limit for working capital loans
questions.explain: 'ASF is calculated on outstanding balance for Term Loans & on sanctioned limit for Working Capital loans', and is payable for NPA accounts too.

questions.q: By what date must the CGFMU guarantee maintenance fee be paid?
questions.explain: Outstanding balances are reported to CGFMU by 31st July, and the fee is paid 'on or before 31st August'.

questions.q: Under CGTMSE, what is the maximum extent of guarantee for women entrepreneurs?
questions.explain: Women entrepreneurs, MSEs in Aspirational Districts, ZED-certified MSEs and SC/ST/PWD entrepreneurs get 85%.

questions.q: Under CGTMSE, what is the extent of guarantee for MSME units in the North East Region (including Sikkim)?
questions.explain: MSME units in the North East Region (incl. Sikkim) are covered at '80% of the amount in default'.

questions.q: How is guarantee cover given under CGFMU?
questions.explain: CGTMSE cover is 'on individual account basis', while CGFMU cover is 'on portfolio basis'.

questions.q: What is the maximum tenure of CGTMSE guarantee cover, including extension?
questions.explain: The initial cover is 5 years or the loan tenure (whichever is lower), extendable by a further 5 years if standard: 'Max. 10 years'.

questions.q: What is the maximum tenure of CGFMU guarantee cover, including extension?
questions.explain: Each CGFMU portfolio is Base Year plus 3 financial years, extendable by a further 3 years if standard: 'Max. 6 years'.

questions.q: Within what period must a CGTMSE credit guarantee be invoked?
options: Within 1 year of the NPA date
Within 3 years of the NPA date or the lock-in period, whichever is later
Within 6 months of the NPA date
questions.explain: 'Invocation of the credit guarantee is to be done within a maximum period of 3 years from NPA date or lock-in period whichever is later.'

questions.q: Under CGTMSE claim pay-out Option 1, how is the claim released?
options: In two instalments: 75% first, the remaining 25% later
questions.explain: Under Option 1, the claim is 'Released in 2 instalments. 1st instalment – 75% of claim pay-out; 2nd instalment – Remaining 25%'.

questions.q: What is the objective of the bank's Risk Management Policy?
options: To remove all risks from banking operations
To implement an effective risk management framework consistent with the bank's policy and operating objectives
questions.explain: The objective is 'to ensure the implementation of an effective risk management framework that is consistent with the Bank achieving its policy and operating objectives'.

questions.q: The Risk Management Policy aims to improve the bank's ability to:
options: Identify, measure and control the overall level of risk taken
questions.explain: The policy 'is aimed to improve the ability to identify, measure and control the overall level of risks undertaken'.

questions.q: Who is mainly responsible for setting risk parameters and an integrated risk management and control system?
questions.explain: 'Primarily responsible for laying down risk parameters and establishing an integrated risk management and control system of the bank is Board of Directors. They are policy approvers.'

questions.q: Who monitors the bank's overall risk management?
options: The Risk Management Committee (RMC), an independent sub-committee of the Board
questions.explain: 'The overall risk management is to be monitored by an Independent Subcommittee of the Board called the Risk Management Committee (RMC).'

questions.q: Which of the following is a function of the Risk Management Committee?
options: Maintaining the CRR and SLR daily
Verifying models used to price complex products
questions.explain: RMC functions include identifying and measuring the risk profile, developing mitigation policies, verifying models used for pricing complex products, reviewing risk models and identifying new risks.

questions.q: Which of these is listed among the broad parameters of the risk management function?
options: Unlimited exposure to a single borrower
Combining risk management with operational departments
A strong MIS for reporting, monitoring and controlling risks
questions.explain: The broad parameters include 'Strong MIS for reporting, monitoring and controlling risks', and a risk framework independent of operational departments.

questions.q: How does the policy define risk?
options: The possibility of loss, financial or to the bank's image or reputation
Only the loss of a loan
questions.explain: 'Risk may be defined as possibility of loss, which may be financial loss or loss to the image or reputation of the Bank.'

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the four commonly referred risks in the policy?
questions.explain: The commonly referred risks are Market Risk, Credit Risk, Operational Risk and Reputational Risk.

questions.q: Market risk arises from adverse changes in:
options: Market variables such as interest rates, exchange rates, equity prices and commodity prices
questions.explain: Market risk arises 'from adverse changes in market variables, such as interest rate, foreign exchange rate, equity price and commodity price'.

questions.q: What has the bank set up to track market risk in real time?
questions.explain: 'The bank has set up an independent Mid Office to track the magnitude of market risk on a real time basis.'

questions.q: Who must approve all of the bank's investments (purchase or sale)?
questions.explain: 'All investments (purchase/sale) of the Bank must be approved by the Investment/Asset Liability Committee.'

questions.q: Which of these is a responsibility of the Investment Cell?
options: Approving all loans above Rs. 1 crore
Maintaining the CRR and SLR without any default
questions.explain: The Investment Cell monitors investment positions daily and 'is also responsible for maintaining CRR & SLR requirements without any default'.

questions.q: The need to replace net outflows from unexpected withdrawal or non-renewal of deposits is called:
questions.explain: 'Funding Risk: Need to replace net outflows due to unanticipated withdrawal/non-renewal of deposits.'

questions.q: The need to make up for expected inflows that do not arrive, such as performing assets turning NPA, is called:
questions.explain: 'Time Risk: Need to compensate for non-receipt of expected inflows of funds, i.e. performing assets turning into non-performing assets.'

questions.q: Liquidity risk from contingent liabilities crystallising is called:
questions.explain: 'Call Risk: Due to crystallization of contingent liabilities and unable to undertake profitable business opportunities when desirable.'

questions.q: Which committee is the top operational unit for managing the balance sheet within the Board's risk parameters?
questions.explain: 'The Asset Liability Management Committee (ALCO) should function as the top operational unit for managing the Balance sheet.'

questions.q: Which two Basel III recommendations does the bank consider the main tools for managing liquidity?
options: The Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) and the Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR)
questions.explain: 'The Bank may consider two of the important recommendations of the Basel 3 committee for liquidity management ... LCR and NSFR.'

questions.q: The LCR makes sure banks have enough high-quality liquid assets to survive an acute stress scenario lasting:
questions.explain: The LCR ensures banks 'have sufficient high quality liquid assets (HQLAs) to survive an acute stress scenario lasting for 30 days'.

questions.q: When are assets considered high-quality liquid assets (HQLA)?
options: When they earn the highest interest
When they have a maturity above 10 years
When they can be easily and immediately converted into cash at little or no loss of value
questions.explain: 'Assets are considered to be high quality liquid assets if they can be easily and immediately converted into cash at little or no loss of value.'

questions.q: How are Level 1 assets included in the stock of HQLA?
options: Without any limit and without any haircut
questions.explain: Level 1 assets 'can be included in the stock of liquid assets without any limit as also without applying any haircut'.

questions.q: Which of these is a Level 1 asset?
options: Cash, including cash reserves above the required CRR
Certificates of deposit issued by banks
questions.explain: Level 1 assets include 'Cash including cash reserves in excess of required CRR' and government securities above the minimum SLR.

questions.q: Level 2 assets can make up at most what share of the overall HQLA stock, after haircuts?
questions.explain: Level 2 assets can be included provided 'they comprise no more than 40% of the overall stock of HQLAs after haircuts'.

questions.q: What minimum haircut applies to the current market value of each Level 2A asset?
questions.explain: 'A minimum 15% haircut should be applied to the current market value of each Level 2A asset.'

questions.q: Which corporate bonds qualify as Level 2A assets?
options: Those rated AAA or above, not issued by a bank, financial institution or NBFC
questions.explain: Level 2A includes 'Corporate bonds, not issued by a bank/financial institution/NBFC ... rated AAA or above by an Eligible Credit Rating Agency'.

questions.q: What must the LCR and NSFR ratios be, per the policy?
questions.explain: The policy states 'The LCR and NSFR ratios must be more than 1'.

questions.q: Under the contingency plan, which source of liquidity may the bank use?
options: Refinance windows of NABARD and the Sponsor Bank
questions.explain: The bank 'may utilize the Liquidity arising out of refinance windows of NABARD and Sponsor Bank', committed lines of credit and similar support.

questions.q: When does price risk occur?
options: When assets are sold before their stated maturity
questions.explain: 'Price risk occurs when assets are sold before their stated maturities.'

questions.q: According to the policy, what is the most important kind of operational risk?
options: Breakdowns in internal controls and corporate governance
Changes in the foreign exchange rate
questions.explain: 'The most important type of operational risk involves breakdowns in internal controls and corporate governance.'

questions.q: Who must carry out post-sanction inspections for all sanctions above Rs. 1 crore and up to Rs. 10 crore?
questions.explain: Regional Managers inspect sanctions of Rs. 50 lakh and above, the General Manager inspects those above Rs. 1 crore up to Rs. 10 crore, and the Chairman inspects those of Rs. 10 crore and above.

questions.q: What are the three key stages of managing the credit portfolio?
options: Pre-sanction appraisal, sanction and disbursal, and post-sanction follow-up and monitoring
questions.explain: 'The management of credit portfolio has three important stages: a) Pre sanction appraisal b) Sanction and disbursal c) Post sanction follow-up and monitoring.'

questions.q: What are non-fund based facilities?
options: Loans disbursed in cash to the borrower
Facilities with no outgo of funds when availed, which may later become a financial liability if the customer fails to honour the commitment
questions.explain: Non-fund based facilities 'do not involve outgo of funds from the bank when the customer avails the facilities but may at a later date crystallise into financial liability'.

questions.q: Which of these is listed as an advantage of non-fund based facilities?
options: A high cost to the banker
questions.explain: Advantages listed: no immediate outlay of funds, future/contingent deployment, earnings by way of commission and fees, deposit mobilisation, easy monitoring, low cost and low probability of default.

questions.q: How does a bank earn from non-fund based facilities?
options: Through up-front commission, fees and exchange income
Through interest on the disbursed amount only
questions.explain: One listed advantage is 'Earnings by way of Up Front commission, fees and exchange income'.

questions.q: Which section of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 defines 'guarantee'?
questions.explain: 'Section 126 of Indian Contract Act, 1872 defines guarantee: A contract to perform the promise or discharge the liability of a third person in case of his default.'

questions.q: In a contract of guarantee, who is the 'applicant'?
options: The person to whom the guarantee is given
The principal debtor, at whose request the guarantee is executed
questions.explain: 'Applicant: The principal debtor: The person at whose request the guarantee is executed.'

questions.q: In a contract of guarantee, who is the 'beneficiary'?
options: The person to whom the guarantee is given, who can enforce it on default
The person who undertakes the obligation
The person who requests the guarantee
questions.explain: 'Beneficiary: The person to whom the guarantee is given and who can enforce it in case of default.'

questions.q: How is a contract of guarantee described in relation to the main contract?
options: As a contract of indemnity under Section 124
As a collateral contract, consequential to the main contract between the applicant and the beneficiary
questions.explain: 'A contract of guarantee is a collateral contract, consequential to a main contract between the applicant and the beneficiary.'

questions.q: A bank guarantee must be unconditional and for a definite:
questions.explain: 'Guarantee issued must be unconditional and for: Definite period, Definite amount, Definite purpose.'

questions.q: A guarantee issued in India, in foreign currency, in favour of a beneficiary in another country is called:
questions.explain: 'Foreign: Issued in India in favour of beneficiary located in any other country in Foreign Currency.'

questions.q: By nature of contract, into which three types are bank guarantees classified?
options: Financial, Performance and Deferred Payment guarantees
questions.explain: 'As per nature of contract, Bank Guarantees are classified in three types: 1) Financial Guarantee 2) Performance Guarantee 3) Deferred Payment Guarantee.'

questions.q: A guarantee issued in place of a cash security or earnest money deposit is a:
questions.explain: 'Financial Guarantees are issued by bank on behalf of customer's requirement to deposit a cash security or earnest money.'

questions.q: A guarantee assuring a third party that the customer will perform the contract as agreed is a:
questions.explain: Performance Guarantees assure 'a third party, that the customer will perform the contract as per condition stipulated in the contract'.

questions.q: A guarantee to suppliers for instalments on capital goods bought on deferred payment terms is a:
questions.explain: Deferred payment guarantees are issued 'in favour of suppliers to guarantee payment of installments for capital goods purchased on deferred payment basis'.

questions.q: Beyond how many days from invocation are branches NOT allowed to postpone payment of a guarantee?
questions.explain: 'Branches are not empowered to postpone beyond 3 days from the date of invocation payment of a guarantee.'

questions.q: What must a branch do before refusing payment on an invoked guarantee?
options: Get permission from its controlling authority
Nothing; it may refuse at will
questions.explain: 'In case the payment is to be refused, controlling authorities permission must be obtained before refusal.'

questions.q: Who must invoke a bank guarantee?
options: Any branch of the issuing bank
The same authority in whose favour the guarantee was issued
questions.explain: 'Invocation has to be made by the same authority in whose favour guarantee is issued.'

questions.q: Which rules govern Letters of Credit in export-import trade?
options: UCPDC 600 of the International Chamber of Commerce
questions.explain: LCs for export-import trade are handled under the 'Uniform Customs and Practice of International Chamber of Commerce (UCPDC 600)'.

questions.q: When did UCPDC 600 come into effect?
questions.explain: 'The ICC Banking Commission approved UCPDC 600 in 25 October 2006, which came into effect from 1st July 2007.'

questions.q: In a letter of credit, who is the beneficiary?
questions.explain: 'The seller or exporter is the beneficiary in whose favour the letter of credit is issued.'

questions.q: Which party opens the letter of credit?
options: The issuing bank, at the request of the applicant (buyer/importer)
questions.explain: 'Issuing Bank is the bank that opens letter of credit', on behalf of the applicant, who is the buyer or importer.

questions.q: Which bank adds its own guarantee to pay or negotiate under the credit?
questions.explain: 'Confirming bank ... confirms and guarantees to undertake the responsibility of payment or negotiation acceptance under the credit.'

questions.q: Which bank is authorised to honour the reimbursement claim for negotiation, payment or acceptance?
questions.explain: 'Reimbursing bank is the party who authorized to honour the reimbursement claim of negotiation/payment/acceptance.'

questions.q: How many parties to a letter of credit are listed in the material?
questions.explain: The parties listed are: Opener/Buyer, Beneficiary/Seller, Issuing Bank, Advising Bank, Confirming Bank, Nominated/Negotiating Bank and Reimbursing Bank.

questions.q: Why is the revocable LC described as obsolete?
options: Because under UCPDC 600 all LCs are irrevocable
Because the RBI banned all LCs
Because it needs three confirming banks
Because it is only for inland trade
questions.explain: 'According to UCPDC 600, all LCs are irrevocable, hence this type of LC is obsolete.'

questions.q: An LC where payment is made after an agreed period, rather than on presentation of documents, is called:
questions.explain: 'Deferred or Usance LC: A letter of credit that ensures payment after a certain period of time.' A sight LC pays on submission of documents.

questions.q: How many times can a transferable LC be transferred?
questions.explain: The second beneficiary 'cannot transfer it further ... It is transferable only once.'

questions.q: Which LC is issued to support intermediary trade, such as by trading houses?
questions.explain: 'Back-to-back is issued to facilitate intermediary trade.'

questions.q: Which LC allows the correspondent bank to give the exporter advances (packing credit) at the issuing bank's responsibility?
questions.explain: 'A Red Clause LC ... has a clause permitting the correspondent bank in the exporter's country to grant advance to beneficiary at issuing bank's responsibility.'

questions.q: A Green Clause LC differs from a Red Clause LC in that it also allows advances for:
questions.explain: 'A Green Clause LC: It permits the advances for storage of goods in a warehouse in addition to preshipment advance.'

questions.q: Which instrument is similar to a performance bond or guarantee but is issued in the form of an LC?
questions.explain: 'Standby Credits: is similar to performance bond or guarantee, but issued in the form of LC.'

questions.q: Where does the MSME sector stand in generating employment at comparatively low capital cost?
questions.explain: The MSME sector generates 'large employment opportunities at comparatively lower capital cost, next only to agriculture'.

questions.q: Which of these is listed as a challenge faced by MSMEs?
questions.explain: The listed challenges include access to affordable finance, delayed payments, marketing constraints, lack of working capital, lack of skilled labour, lack of real-time support and lack of infrastructure.

questions.q: How many credit-linked Government schemes does the JanSamarth Portal link on a single platform?
questions.explain: JanSamarth is 'a unique digital portal linking fourteen Credit Linked Government schemes on a single platform'.

questions.q: Which of these schemes is linked on the JanSamarth Portal?
questions.explain: The listed JanSamarth schemes include Weaver Mudra Scheme, PMMY, Stand Up India, PMEGP, SRMS and PM SVANidhi.

questions.q: Which statutory body under the MSME Ministry promotes khadi and village industries for rural employment?
questions.explain: 'Khadi and Village Industries Commission (KVIC) is a statutory organisation engaged in promoting and developing khadi and village industries for providing employment opportunities in rural areas.'

questions.q: In which year was the National Small Industries Corporation Limited (NSIC) established?
questions.explain: 'Established in 1955, the National Small Industries Corporation Limited (NSIC) is responsible for promoting, aiding and fostering growth of micro and small enterprises.'

questions.q: In which year was the National Institute for MSME (NI-MSME) established?
questions.explain: 'Established in 1960, the National Institute for Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (NI-MSME) is responsible for enterprise promotion and entrepreneurship development.'

questions.q: What does MGIRI stand for?
options: Mahatma Gandhi Institute for Rural Industrialisation
MSME Growth and Industrial Rural Initiative
Mahatma Gandhi Institute of Rural Innovation
questions.explain: The statutory bodies slide lists the 'Mahatma Gandhi Institute for Rural Industrialisation (MGIRI)'.

questions.q: How many District Industries Centres (DICs) are there in Tamil Nadu, per the material?
questions.explain: 'The District Industries Centers located in 38 districts of Tamilnadu' support entrepreneurs.

questions.q: Which portal lets micro and small enterprises file applications online about delayed payments?
questions.explain: 'MSME SAMADHAAN is a portal ... where Micro and Small enterprises can file their applications online regarding delayed payments.'

questions.q: To whom are MSME SAMADHAAN applications forwarded automatically?
options: The Micro and Small Enterprise Facilitation Council (MSEFC) of the State/UT
questions.explain: Applications are 'forwarded automatically to the concerned Micro and Small Enterprise Facilitation Council (MSEFC)'.

questions.q: What is mandatory for using the MSME SAMADHAAN service?
questions.explain: 'UDYAM registration is mandatory for availing this service.'

questions.q: After how many days of delayed payment can an MSE approach the Facilitation Council?
questions.explain: 'In case of delay in payments beyond 45 days, the MSE may approach the Council for dispute resolution.'

questions.q: On delayed payment to an MSE, what interest is the buyer liable to pay?
options: Compound interest at 3 times the RBI Bank Rate
Simple interest at the repo rate
Compound interest at 2 times the repo rate
questions.explain: 'The buyer is liable to pay compound interest on the amount at the 3 times of the Bank Rate notified by RBI.'

questions.q: Within what period must every reference to the MSEFC be decided?
questions.explain: 'Every reference to the MSEFC shall be decided within a period of 90 days from the date of making reference.'

questions.q: Before appealing an MSEFC award, what share of the award must the appellant (not being the supplier) deposit?
questions.explain: No appeal is entertained 'unless the appellant (not being the supplier) has deposited with it the 75% of the award amount'.

questions.q: When was the MSME Sambandh portal launched?
questions.explain: 'The M/o MSME had launched MSME Sambandh Portal on 8th December, 2017.'

questions.q: Under the Public Procurement Policy, what share of annual procurement must come from MSEs?
questions.explain: Annual procurement goals: 25% from MSEs, of which 4% from MSEs owned by SC/ST and 3% from MSEs owned by women.

questions.q: From what date did the Public Procurement Policy for MSEs become mandatory?
questions.explain: The policy 'is effective from 1st April, 2012 and has become mandatory w.e.f. 1st April, 2015'.

questions.q: What is the size of the Self Reliant India (SRI) Fund of Funds for MSMEs?
questions.explain: The Government announced a '10,000 crore Fund of Funds for MSME', called the Self Reliant India (SRI) Fund.

questions.q: Under the amended Global Tender Rule (GFR 2017), for tenders up to what value can a Global Tender Enquiry not be invited without prior approval?
questions.explain: 'No Global Tender Enquiry (GTE) to be invited for tenders up to 200 Crores without prior approval.'

questions.q: Under the Public Procurement (Preference to Make in India) Order, a 'Class I Supplier' has local content of:
questions.explain: 'Class I Supplier – 50% or more local content; Class II Supplier – 20% to 50%; Non Local Supplier – 20% or less.'

questions.q: MSME SAMPARK is a:
options: Job portal connecting job seekers from MSME tool rooms and technical institutions with recruiters
questions.explain: The MSME Sampark job portal, launched on 27.06.2018, is a platform where job seekers and recruiters register for mutual benefit.

questions.q: What does CHAMPIONS stand for?
options: Centre for Helping All MSMEs to Prosper In Our National Sector
Common Help And Mentoring Platform for Industry
Credit, Handholding and Marketing Portal for Indian MSMEs
Creation and Harmonious Application of Modern Processes for Increasing the Output and National Strength
questions.explain: The material gives this full form for CHAMPIONS.

questions.q: When was the CHAMPIONS portal launched?
questions.explain: 'CHAMPIONS portal launched on 1st June, 2020.'

questions.q: In the CHAMPIONS hub-and-spoke model, where is the hub located?
options: The office of the Ministry of MSME, New Delhi
questions.explain: 'The hub is situated in the office of M/o MSME, New Delhi while the spokes are located in the States and UTs.'

questions.q: Where are Tamil Nadu's two CHAMPIONS state control rooms?
questions.explain: 'Tamil Nadu is having 2 state control rooms in Tirunelveli & Thoothukudi.'

questions.q: When was the Government e-Marketplace (GeM) launched?
questions.explain: GeM, 'a one-stop online procurement portal for all Government Buyers', was 'Launched on 9th August 2016'.

questions.q: Which GFR rule was amended to make procurement through GeM mandatory for goods and services available on it?
questions.explain: 'Rule 149 of GFR amended to: Procurement of Goods and Services by Ministries or Department will be mandatory for Goods or Services available on GeM.'

questions.q: What is the purpose of TReDS (Trade Receivables Discounting System)?
options: To resolve delayed-payment disputes through MSEFC
To help MSMEs unlock working capital by converting receivables into cash
questions.explain: 'TReDS is an online platform set up to facilitate MSMEs to unlock working capital by converting their receivables into cash.'

quizzes.topic: TNGB Capital Budgeting Techniques for Project Appraisal 2026

questions.q: Why are capital budgeting techniques required?
options: To find out whether the chosen project is viable and will earn enough return on the investment
To fix the bank's deposit rates
To calculate a borrower's income tax
questions.explain: Capital budgeting is required 'To ascertain, the chosen project is viable & will generate sufficient return over investment.'

questions.q: Which of the following is a traditional (non-discounting) method of evaluating profitability?
questions.explain: The traditional/non-discounting methods are the Payback Period and the Average Rate of Return. NPV, BCR and IRR are discounting methods.

questions.q: Which of the following is a discounting method?
questions.explain: The discounting methods listed are 1. NPV, 2. BCR and 3. IRR.

questions.q: What does the payback period measure?
options: The time needed to recover the original investment
The total profit over the project's life
The ratio of benefits to costs
The interest rate at which NPV is zero
questions.explain: 'Payback Period: Length of time required to recover the original investment.'

questions.q: In the payback example, Rs. 1,00,000 is invested, inflows up to year 5 total Rs. 88,000, and year 6 brings Rs. 30,000. What is the payback period?
questions.explain: Year 6 gives Rs. 2,500 per month (Rs. 30,000 / 12). Five months' return is Rs. 12,500, so Rs. 88,000 + Rs. 12,500 = Rs. 1,00,500, a payback of 5 years 5 months.

questions.q: How is the Average Rate of Return calculated?
options: Present value of inflows / Initial investment
Average net operating profit / Average investment made in the unit
questions.explain: 'Avg. ROR = Avg. of Net Operating Profit / Avg. of investment made in the unit.'

questions.q: In the example, Projects A and B both give an average return of 11.40%. Which is more profitable, and why?
options: Project A, because it gives 11.40% in 6 years while Project B takes 7 years
Project B, because its total profit is higher
questions.explain: Project A 'Gets 11.40% return in 6 Yrs. But Project B gets the same return in 7 Yrs.'

questions.q: Why are discounting techniques preferred in industry?
options: Because they ignore future cash flows
Because they take the time value of money into account
Because they use accounting profit only
Because they are the simplest to calculate
questions.explain: 'Discounting techniques are the most preferable in the industry ... Time value of money is considered here.'

questions.q: What is the opposite of 'discounting'?
questions.explain: The material states 'The opposite term of discounting is Compounding.'

questions.q: At 10% interest, what will Rs. 1,00,000 grow to at the end of 2 years?
questions.explain: The compounding example shows Year 1: Rs. 1,10,000, Year 2: Rs. 1,21,000, Year 3: Rs. 1,33,100.

questions.q: What is the formula for compounding?
questions.explain: 'Compounding: FV = PV (1 + k)^n', where FV is future value, PV present value, k the rate of interest and n the number of years.

questions.q: In the discounting example, what is the discounting factor for year 1 at 10%?
questions.explain: The table gives DF @ 10% for Year 1 as 0.909 (100/110), Year 2 as 0.826 and Year 3 as 0.751.

questions.q: What is the discounting factor for year 1 at 15%?
questions.explain: The table gives DF @ 15% for Year 1 as 0.870 (100/115), Year 2 as 0.756 and Year 3 as 0.658.

questions.q: How is Net Present Value (NPV) calculated?
options: Present value of cash inflows minus cash outflow (investment)
questions.explain: 'NPV = Cash inflow (Profit) – Cash outflow (Investment)', with inflows discounted to present value.

questions.q: In the NPV example (investment Rs. 1,00,000, discounted at 16%), the total present value of inflows is Rs. 1,04,510. What is the NPV?
questions.explain: 'NPV = Rs. 104510 – Rs. 100000 = Rs. 4510.' Cash flow generated is more than the money invested, so the project is viable.

questions.q: What discount rate is used in the NPV illustration?
questions.explain: The illustration asks to 'Calculate NPV @16.00% return'.

questions.q: How is the Benefit Cost Ratio (BCR) calculated?
options: Initial investment / Present value of returns
Present value of returns / Initial investment
questions.explain: 'BCR = PV of returns / Initial investment = Cash inflow / Cash outflow.'

questions.q: In the example, BCR = 1,04,510 / 1,00,000 = 1.04. What does this show?
options: The project is marginal, because BCR equals 1
The project is financially viable, because BCR is more than 1
Nothing; BCR is not used for decisions
The project is not viable, because BCR is near 1
questions.explain: 'BCR > 1, so the project is financially viable.'

questions.q: What is the Internal Rate of Return (IRR)?
options: The rate at which BCR becomes 2
The discount rate at which NPV becomes zero
questions.explain: 'IRR is a discount rate at which NPV becomes Zero.'

questions.q: When should a project be accepted on the basis of IRR?
options: When IRR is greater than the cost of capital or opportunity cost of capital
When IRR equals the inflation rate
When IRR is less than the cost of capital
questions.explain: 'Accept the project when IRR > Capital cost (or) Opportunity cost of capital. Reject the project when IRR < Capital cost.'

questions.q: When several projects are otherwise similar, which should be chosen?
options: The one with the highest IRR
The one with the longest payback period
The one with the lowest IRR
The one with the lowest BCR
questions.explain: 'If all the other factors are same for different projects then the project with the Highest Internal rate of return value should be considered.'

questions.q: In the milk-processing example, the debt-equity ratio is 3:1, debt costs 16% and equity's opportunity cost is 15%. What is the cost of capital?
In the milk-processing example, Mr. X could invest in a mutual fund earning 15%. What is that 15% called?
questions.explain: 'The return from missed out/lost option is an opportunity cost.' Here the mutual fund return of 15% is the opportunity cost.

questions.q: What IRR is calculated in the milk-processing example?
questions.explain: IRR = 15 + (5 × 69,100) / 1,10,650 = 15 + 3.12 = 18.12%, which exceeds both the cost of capital (15.75%) and the opportunity cost (15%).

questions.q: According to the decision table, when is a project 'Marginal'?
options: When NPV is negative and BCR is below one
When IRR is above the lending rate
When NPV is zero, BCR is one and IRR equals the lending rate
When NPV is positive and BCR is above one
questions.explain: The decision table: Feasible = positive NPV, BCR > 1, IRR > lending rate; Marginal = NPV 0, BCR 1, IRR = lending rate; Not feasible = negative NPV, BCR < 1, IRR < lending rate.

questions.q: What is the Break Even Point (BEP)?
options: The point at which profit is highest
The point at which total revenue equals total cost, with no profit and no loss
The point at which NPV is highest
The point at which the loan is fully repaid
questions.explain: 'BEP at which total revenue & total cost are equal. No loss / No gain.'

questions.q: Which of these is a fixed cost, according to the BEP slide?
questions.explain: 'Fixed cost – Remains the same regardless of product's output like lease & rental Exp, Ins & Int payout.' Labour and production charges are variable costs.

questions.q: Mr. Y's fixed cost is Rs. 3,00,000, his variable cost is Rs. 55/kg and the selling price is Rs. 60/kg. What is his break-even quantity?
How is the Debt Service Coverage Ratio (DSCR) calculated?
options: (Net profit + Depreciation + Interest expense) / Total repayment (principal + interest)
questions.explain: 'DSCR = Net profit + Depreciation + Interest Exp / Total Repayment (P + I).'

questions.q: What DSCR is required, per the material, and to which loans does DSCR apply?
questions.explain: 'DSCR is applicable for Term loans only. Required DSCR is 1.50. If it is > 2.00, the project is more viable.'

questions.q: What is the Repo Rate?
options: The rate at which the RBI rediscounts bills of exchange
The rate at which banks lend to their best customers
The rate at which the RBI accepts uncollateralised deposits from banks
The rate at which the RBI provides liquidity under the LAF against government and other approved securities
questions.explain: 'Repo Rate refers to the interest rate at which the Reserve Bank provides liquidity under the liquidity adjustment facility (LAF) to every LAF participant against the collateral of government and other approved securities.'

questions.q: What is the Standing Deposit Facility (SDF) rate?
options: The rate at which the RBI accepts uncollateralised overnight deposits from LAF participants
The rate at which the RBI rediscounts commercial paper
The rate at which banks borrow by dipping into their SLR
The rate paid on CRR balances
questions.explain: 'On an overnight basis, SDF is the rate at which the Reserve Bank accepts the uncollateralised deposits from all LAF participants.'

questions.q: When was the SDF introduced, and what did it replace as the floor of the LAF corridor?
options: April 2022; the fixed reverse repo rate
questions.explain: 'Since SDF was introduced in April 2022, it replaced the fixed reverse repo rate as the floor of the LAF corridor.'

questions.q: What is the Marginal Standing Facility (MSF)?
options: The rate at which the RBI absorbs liquidity without collateral
A penal overnight rate at which banks can borrow from the RBI by dipping into their SLR portfolio up to a limit
questions.explain: MSF is 'the penal rate at which banks can borrow from the Reserve Bank by plunging into their Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) portfolio up to a predefined limit', acting as a safety valve.

questions.q: In the LAF corridor, which rate is the upper bound (ceiling)?
questions.explain: 'LAF corridor has the marginal standing facility (MSF) rate as its upper bound, ceiling, and the standing deposit facility (SDF) rate as the lower bound, floor, and the policy repo rate is in the middle.'

questions.q: Which rate is in the middle of the LAF corridor?
questions.explain: The policy repo rate is 'in the middle of the corridor', between SDF (floor) and MSF (ceiling).

questions.q: What is the RBI's main liquidity management tool for frictional liquidity needs?
options: A 14-day variable-rate term repo/reverse repo auction aligned with the CRR maintenance cycle
questions.explain: The main liquidity management tool is 'a 14-day term repo/reverse repo auction operation at a variable rate ... conducted to overlap with the cash reserve ratio (CRR) maintenance cycle'.

questions.q: Apart from the LAF, which of these is an instrument of liquidity management?
questions.explain: 'Apart from LAF, the other instruments of liquidity management include forex swaps, outright open market operations (OMOs), and the market stabilisation scheme (MSS).'

questions.q: What is the primary objective of the RBI's monetary policy?
options: Maintaining price stability, while keeping growth in mind
questions.explain: 'The primary objective of the RBI's monetary policy is to maintain price stability while keeping in mind the objective of growth.'

questions.q: Under which section of the RBI Act, 1934 was the Monetary Policy Committee constituted?
questions.explain: 'MPC was constituted as per Section 45ZB of RBI Act 1934.'

questions.q: How many members does the Monetary Policy Committee have?
options: 6: 3 from the RBI and 3 nominated by the Government of India
5: 3 from the RBI and 2 from the Government
7: 4 from the RBI and 3 from the Government
questions.explain: 'Members: 6 members including RBI Governor (3 from RBI & 3 GOI nominated members).'

questions.q: Who chairs the MPC, and what happens in case of a tie?
options: The RBI Governor chairs it and has a casting vote
The Finance Minister chairs it and has a casting vote
The Deputy Governor chairs it; ties are decided by lot
The senior-most member chairs it; a tie means no decision
questions.explain: 'RBI Governor shall be the Chair Person of MPC & shall have casting vote, in case of tie.'

questions.q: How often is the MPC presently held?
questions.explain: 'Presently, MPC is being held on bi-monthly basis.'

questions.q: What inflation target has been given to the MPC for 2021–2026?
questions.explain: 'Inflation target given to MPC for the period 2021–2026 is 4% (+ or – 2%) (Minimum 2% & maximum 6%).'

questions.q: An expansionary (easy money) policy is used during:
options: High inflation, to reduce money supply
Low economic growth, to boost the economy
questions.explain: 'Expansionary policy during low economic growth time, to boost the economic growth & stimulate the economy by reducing CRR/SLR/Repo Rate etc.'

questions.q: Which of the following is an expansionary monetary policy tool?
questions.explain: The expansionary tools slide lists: 1. Decrease interest rate, 2. Reduce reserve requirements, 3. Expand open market operations.

questions.q: A contractionary ('dear money' or 'tight money') policy is used to:
options: Take excess money out of the market during inflation, by raising CRR, SLR, repo rate etc.
questions.explain: 'Contractionary policy during inflation times to take out the excess money from the market by increasing CRR/SLR/Repo Rate etc.'

questions.q: What is the Bank Rate?
options: The rate at which the RBI will buy or rediscount bills of exchange or commercial papers
The rate at which banks accept deposits
questions.explain: 'Bank rate is the rate at which the Reserve Bank is willing to purchase or rediscount bills of exchange or other commercial papers.'

questions.q: Under which section of the RBI Act is the Bank Rate published, and which rate is it aligned with?
questions.explain: 'The Bank Rate was published under Section 49 of the RBI Act, 1934, and the rate has been aligned with the MSF rate.'

questions.q: The Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) is a percentage of a bank's:
questions.explain: CRR is 'the average daily balance a bank is mandated to maintain with the Reserve Bank as a per cent of its net demand and time liabilities (NDTL)'.

questions.q: In which assets is the SLR typically maintained?
options: Unencumbered government securities, cash and gold
questions.explain: SLR assets 'typically ... should be in unencumbered government securities, cash and gold'.

questions.q: What are Open Market Operations (OMOs)?
options: Overnight lending to banks against SLR securities
Uncollateralised deposits taken by the RBI
The RBI's outright purchase or sale of government securities to inject or absorb durable liquidity
questions.explain: 'OMOs include outright purchase/sale of government securities by the Reserve Bank for injection and/or absorption of durable liquidity.'

questions.q: According to the policy rates 'as on 5 June 2026' in the material, what is the Repo Rate?
questions.explain: The material lists Repo Rate: 5.25%, SDF: 5%, MSF: 5.50%, Bank Rate: 5.50%, Reverse Repo: 3.35%, CRR: 3%, SLR: 18%.

questions.q: According to the policy rates 'as on 5 June 2026' in the material, what is the CRR?
questions.explain: The material lists 'CRR: 3%' among the policy rates as on 5 June 2026.

questions.q: According to the policy rates 'as on 5 June 2026' in the material, what is the SLR?
questions.explain: The material lists 'SLR Rate: 18.00%'.

questions.q: What is the maturity range of Treasury Bills?
questions.explain: 'Treasury bills (T BILL) are the shortest-term government investment and mature in four weeks to one year.'

questions.q: When were Treasury Bills first issued in India?
questions.explain: 'Treasury Bills were first issued in India in 1917.' The active T-Bills now are 91-day, 182-day and 364-day.

questions.q: Borrowing or lending for 2 to 14 days in the money market is called:
questions.explain: Call money is 1 day, notice money is 2–14 days, and term money is more than 14 days.

questions.q: What is the maturity range of commercial paper?
questions.explain: 'Maturities on commercial paper range from one to 270 days, with an average of around 30 days.'

questions.q: How is a Certificate of Participation secured, unlike a bond issued by the same agency?
questions.explain: A Certificate of Participation 'is different from a bond issued by these agencies since participation certificates are secured by lease revenues'.

quizzes.topic: Government Schemes 2026 – Important Terms and Conditions

questions.q: Under the Agricultural Marketing Infrastructure (AMI) scheme, what is the minimum margin?
questions.explain: AMI: 'Margin – Min 20% of TFO (Total Financial Outlay)', and the term loan should not be less than 50% of project cost.

questions.q: Under AMI, what subsidy rate applies to FPOs, SHGs, women, SC and ST beneficiaries?
questions.explain: AMI subsidy: '33.33% – FPO, SHG, Women, SC & ST (Max Rs. 100 L – Storage & Rs. 30 L – Non Storage); 25.00% – Others'.

questions.q: What is the implementation period of the Agriculture Infrastructure Fund (AIF/NAIFF)?
questions.explain: 'NAIFF / AIF – Impl period – 2020-21 to 2032-33'.

questions.q: What interest subvention does the AIF offer?
options: 3% per annum, up to a loan limit of Rs. 2 crore
3% per annum, up to Rs. 5 crore
2% per annum, up to Rs. 1 crore
questions.explain: 'Interest subvention of 3% per annum up to a limit of Rs. 2 crore', for a maximum of 7 years including 2 years moratorium.

questions.q: Under AIF, who pays the CGTMSE credit guarantee fee for loans up to Rs. 2 crore?
questions.explain: 'Credit guarantee coverage will be available ... under CGTMSE scheme for a loan up to Rs. 2 crore. The fee for this coverage will be paid by the Government.'

questions.q: What is the minimum membership of a Farmer Producer Organisation in plain areas?
questions.explain: 'Min members – 300 (for Plain Areas); Hilly/Northeastern States – 100.'

questions.q: What equity grant is available to an FPO?
options: Up to Rs. 2,000 per farmer, with a maximum of Rs. 15 lakh per FPO
Up to Rs. 1,000 per farmer, with no maximum
Up to Rs. 5,000 per farmer, with a maximum of Rs. 10 lakh
questions.explain: 'Equity Grant is available up to Rs. 2000/- per farmer max of Rs. 15 Lakhs per FPO', paid by SFAC in 3 tranches.

questions.q: Under the Agri Clinics and Agri Business Centres (ACABC) scheme, what subsidy applies to women, SC/ST and NER beneficiaries?
questions.explain: ACABC subsidy is '44% for Women/SC/ST/NER & 36% for Others', with a lock-in period of 3 years.

questions.q: Under KCC, up to what loan limit is no collateral required?
questions.explain: 'KCC without collateral for loan limits of up to Rs. 2 lakh. For loan limits up to Rs. 3 lakh, collateral can be waived in tie-up arrangements.'

questions.q: Under KCC, what Prompt Repayment Incentive (PRI) is given to farmers?
questions.explain: KCC: 'IS – 1.50% to lenders; PRI – 3.00% to farmers'.

questions.q: Under PMEGP, what subsidy does a general-category beneficiary get in a rural area?
questions.explain: PMEGP subsidy: General – 15% urban, 25% rural; Special – 25% urban, 35% rural.

questions.q: Under PMEGP, what is the beneficiary contribution for the special category?
questions.explain: 'Beneficiary contribution (own investment) is 10% for the general category and 5% for the special category.'

questions.q: Under PMEGP, what is the maximum project cost for a manufacturing unit?
questions.explain: 'Maximum Project Cost For Manufacturing – Rs. 50.00 lakh and for Services – Rs. 20.00 lakh.'

questions.q: Under UYEGP, what is the maximum project cost?
questions.explain: 'UYEGP – Max. Project Cost – Rs. 15.00 lakh – Only Trading/Business.'

questions.q: Under UYEGP, what is the maximum family income allowed?
questions.explain: 'Family income – should not be more than Rs. 8.00 lakh.'

questions.q: Under PMFME, what subsidy can an individual get?
options: 15%, up to a maximum of Rs. 5 lakh
35%, up to a maximum of Rs. 10 lakh
25%, up to a maximum of Rs. 75 lakh
35%, up to a maximum of Rs. 3 crore
questions.explain: PMFME: Individual – 35% (Max Rs. 10 L), margin 10%; Group – 35% (Max Rs. 3 cr), margin 10%.

questions.q: Which concept is promoted under PMFME?
questions.explain: 'ODOP – One District One Product concept is promoted' under PMFME.

questions.q: What is the loan range under the Stand Up India scheme?
questions.explain: Stand Up India: 'Loan amount between Rs. 10.00 lakh and Rs. 1.00 cr.'

questions.q: For a non-individual enterprise under Stand Up India, what minimum stake must women or SC/ST entrepreneurs hold?
questions.explain: 'If it is a non individual enterprise min 51% of the stake should be borne by women entrepreneur/SC/ST.'

questions.q: Under MUDRA, which category covers loans above Rs. 50,000 and up to Rs. 5 lakh?
questions.explain: Shishu – up to Rs. 50,000; Kishore – above Rs. 50,000 up to Rs. 5 lakh; Tarun – above Rs. 5 lakh to Rs. 10 lakh; Tarun Plus – Rs. 10 lakh to Rs. 20 lakh.

questions.q: What margin applies to a Tarun Plus MUDRA loan?
questions.explain: MUDRA margin: Shishu – Nil; Kishore – 10%; Tarun – 15%; Tarun Plus – 20%.

questions.q: Under PM SVANidhi, what interest subsidy is given on regular repayment?
questions.explain: PM SVANidhi gives 'interest subsidy @ 7% per annum on regular repayment of loan'.

questions.q: Under PM SVANidhi, what is the first loan tranche amount and term?
questions.explain: '1st dose – Rs. 15000/- with 12 months term; 2nd dose – Rs. 25000/- with 18 months; 3rd dose – Rs. 50000/- with 36 months.'

questions.q: Under the NEEDS scheme, what is the maximum subsidy?
questions.explain: NEEDS: projects from Rs. 10 lakh to Rs. 5 crore; 'Subsidy 25% max of Rs. 75 lakh'; plus 3% interest subvention throughout repayment.

questions.q: Under TAHDCO, what is the maximum annual family income allowed?
questions.explain: TAHDCO eligibility: 'The annual family income of the applicant should not exceed Rs. 3.00 lakh.'

questions.q: Under the Weavers Credit Card (WCC), what is the maximum loan?
questions.explain: 'WCC (Weavers Credit Card) ... Max loan – Rs. 2.00 lakh. Margin – 20% on project cost.'

questions.q: In SHG financing, what is the first-dose loan amount?
options: 8 times the existing corpus or Rs. 3 lakh, whichever is higher
6 times the existing corpus or Rs. 1.50 lakh, whichever is higher
questions.explain: 'First Dose: 6 times of the existing corpus or minimum of Rs. 1.50 lakh, whichever is higher.'

questions.q: When was the PM Vishwakarma scheme launched?
questions.explain: 'PM-Vishwakarma – Launched on September 17, 2023', with the Ministry of MSME as nodal agency and an initial outlay of Rs. 13,000 crores.

questions.q: Under PM Vishwakarma, what is the first loan amount and its repayment period?
questions.explain: 'First Loan – Rs. 1,00,000/- (Repayment – 18 months); Second Loan – Rs. 2,00,000/- (Repayment – 30 months).'

questions.q: Under the Annal Ambedkar Business Championship Scheme (AABCS), what capital subsidy is available?
questions.explain: AABCS gives '35% capital subsidy (Not exceeding Rs. 1.5 crore) on eligible project cost – Front end' to 100% SC/ST-owned enterprises.

questions.q: Indian banks' existing compliance processes follow the recommendations of which report?
questions.explain: Banks have compliance processes 'in accordance with the recommendations of the Ghosh Committee report of 1992'.

questions.q: Which BCBS document says the compliance function must be adequately enabled and sufficiently independent?
options: The BCBS paper on Compliance and the Compliance Function in Banks (April 2005)
questions.explain: The Basel Committee on Banking Supervision document of April 2005 'essentially articulates this perception'.

questions.q: Observing the RBI Act, RRB Act, FEMA and PMLA falls under which type of compliance?
